title: Art Rupe's hard bargains and the gospel group's advance
summary: Rupe reported sales honestly but was miserly, adding a contract clause so a gospel group earned no royalties until an advance for a broken-down car was repaid.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Who are some of the record people that you most respected? I mean, the out-of-town guys that came in. That I'm most respected? Yeah, that you most respected who came in.

Well, I have to qualify almost everybody. For instance, let's say Art Roop. Okay. One of the really big ones. I have no doubt in my mind, or I could be wrong, but I have no doubt in my mind that Art Roop reported sales correctly. Mm-hmm. That Art Roop was not a person who would sell X number of records and sell... Tell you... Tell you he sold half that.
But he drove a hard bargain. He was a miserly guy to work out a contract with. Mm-hmm. And he didn't mind if you were in a bind, taking advantage of that bind.

Okay. For instance, he had a great gospel group. And he literally... The guys, they were traveling in a big Cadillac limousine, and the limousine broke down, and it was really bad. He had to... I think it caught fire or something. And he had to get another car. And Art wired him to me. And Art wired him to money, wired it to me.

And dictated a contract thing, a thing, a page thing to add to his contract, which said that until he paid back the money, he not only didn't get his royalties, he didn't earn any. If you appreciate the difference. In other words... You know what I'm saying?
Yeah. Yeah. Okay. Of course, it's a big difference. Yeah. In other words, your royalties are not going back to pay for this.
You've got to earn the money somewhere else to pay for this sucker. Right. And in the meantime, you're not getting any... Right.
